A Comprehensive Mechanistic Scenario for Asymmetric Cross-
Coupling Reaction of Diazoacetate and Terminal Alkyne under
Copper Catalysis
Yan-Kun Cui, Sai-Bo Cao, and Yang Wang*
Cite This: Inorg. Chem. 2025, 64, 24012−24019

ABSTRACT: Terminal alkynes have emerged as highly versatile
building blocks for constructing C−C bonds. These compounds are
thought to undergo conversion to acetylide intermediates before
further transformation. In the present work, the possible reaction
mechanisms of the cross-coupling reaction of diazoacetate with
alkyne under copper catalysis are investigated using the M06-L
method. Two different reaction pathways including a copper−
acetylide mechanism and a copper−carbene mechanism are
investigated and comparatively analyzed. Computational results
demonstrate that the energetically favored pathway follows a copper-acetylide mechanism, comprising alkynation of the terminal
alkyne, carbenation, carbene insertion, Aldol reaction, and catalyst regeneration. In contrast, the alternative pathway involving a
carbenation−alkynation sequence is found to be less favorable. The rate-determining step is verified by the carbenation process,
which also determines the stereoselectivity. Noncovalent interaction (NCI) analysis reveals that noncovalent interactions between
the diazo and indane groups of the bisoxazoline ligand are important in controlling stereoselectivity. Calculations involving a series of
chiral ligands further demonstrate that the bulky indane moiety in the bisoxazoline ligand is essential for achieving stereoselectivity,
consistent with experimental observations.
1. INTRODUCTION
Terminal alkynes have garnered significant interest due to their
distinctive structural characteristics and high reactivity, making
them highly versatile building blocks for constructing C−C
bonds. These compounds are typically converted into acetylide
intermediates prior to further transformation.
1−5
Trans-
formation of terminal alkynes represents one of the most
effective strategies to construct multifunctional molecules from
simple precursors under transition-metal catalysis.
6−14
An
alkyne−metal complex forms through the coordination of a
transition metal to the alkyne triple bond. This interaction
weakens the triple bond and facilitates subsequent nucleophilic
attack, leading to the formation of a vinylmetal species
(Scheme 1). Additionally, this metal coordination enhances
the acidity of the terminal hydrogen, enabling deprotonation to
form an alkynyl−metal species.
Copper salts, valued for their low cost and minimal toxicity,
are extensively employed in organic transformations.
15−22
Among their applications, copper-catalyzed cross-coupling
reactions involving terminal alkynes are well-established, and
numerous strategies have been devised for the construction of
allenes.
23−30
Recently, Sun et al. reported a tandem cross-
coupling/alkynylogous aldol reaction between terminal alkyne
and diazoacetate catalyzed by copper species for the synthesis
of tetrasubstituted allenes (Scheme 2).
31
This method affords
the products in a high yield (87%, Scheme 2) with excellent
enantioselectivity (97% ee, Scheme 2) and diastereoselectivity
(>19:1 dr, Scheme 2), representing an efficient approach for
the enantioselective synthesis of tetrasubstituted allenes
bearing both central and axial chirality.
The catalytic copper species typically activates the terminal
alkyne to produce a copper−acetylide species and also
activates the diazoacetate to produce a copper−carbene

species. Terminal alkyne undergoes deprotonation to deliver
the copper−acetylide, which subsequently reacts with the
diazoacetate. Alternatively, the copper catalyst may first
activate the diazoacetate to produce the copper−carbene,
which then engages with the terminal alkyne. Although Sun
and co-workers have made significant progress to elucidate the
mechanism of this reaction, two major problems are still
unclear. First, establishing a general mechanistic scheme is
challenging due to the involvement of different activation
modes. Second, the molecular origin of the high stereo-
selectivity requires further clarification. As a result, our interest
was drawn to investigating this copper-catalyzed asymmetric
synthesis of a tetrasubstituted allene. Theoretical mechanistic
analysis of transition-metal-catalyzed reactions
32−37
is at the
center of our research. Therefore, in this study, we employed
density functional theory (DFT), which is a robust computa-
tional method for mechanistic investigations,
38−49
to theoret-
ically investigate the mechanism of the copper-catalyzed cross-
coupling reaction between a terminal alkyne and diazoacetate.
In particular, we intend to elucidate the activation mode in
detail, specifically whether copper−acetylide or copper−
carbene serves as the key intermediate.
2. COMPUTATIONAL METHODS
All quantum chemical calculations were performed using the Gaussian
09 software package.
50
Geometry optimizations were carried out with
the M06-L functional.
51,52
The 6-31G(d, p) basis set
53,54
was
employed for the C, H, O, N, and F atoms, while the SDD basis
set
55,56
was used for the Cu atom. Solvation effects were incorporated
via the continuum solvation model IEF-PCM,
57,58
using dichloro-
methane (DCM, ε = 8.93) as the solvent. Harmonic vibrational
analysis verifies that the stationary points are characterized as minima
with no imaginary frequency or transition states with one and only
one imaginary frequency, respectively. To refine the calculated energy,
single-point calculations with a larger basis set were then performed
based on these optimized structures, by using the M06-L functional
with the Def2-TZVP basis set.
59,60
The free energies reported in this
work were calculated based on the single point energy at the M06-L/
def2-TZVP level, including the Gibbs free energy thermal correction
obtained from vibrational analysis at the geometry optimization level.
For disclosing the origin of stereoselectivity, the Multiwfn software
package
61
is used to generate the interaction wave functions, which
are then visualized through VMD.
62
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Reaction Mechanism. Considering the behavior of
copper species, we propose both the copper−acetylide
mechanism and the copper−carbene mechanism on the
copper-catalyzed reaction between diazoacetate and alkyne,
as illustrated in Scheme 3. Both pathways were initiated from
the Cu-I species. In the copper−acetylide mechanism, the
sequential base-assisted deprotonation and alkynation of
alkyne 1a deliver the copper−acetylide intermediate Int-I.
Subsequent carbenation between Int-I and diazoacetate 2a
affords the copper−carbene acetylide species Int-II. Alter-
natively, in the copper−carbene mechanism, Int-II is generated
via an alternate route involving initial carbenation of the
intermediate Cu-I, accompanied by deprotonation of alkyne
1a. Insertion of the carbene moiety into the acetylide then
yields propargyl copper intermediate Int-III. An alkynylogous
aldol reaction then occurs, leading to allenoate copper species
Int-IV. Protonation of Int-IV delivers the final chiral exocyclic
α-allenol and regenerates the active copper species. With these
proposed mechanisms in hand, theoretical calculations were
conducted to elucidate the detailed mechanism of the Cu(I)-
catalyzed cross-coupling reaction between diazoacetate and
alkyne.
3.1.1. Copper−Acetylide Mechanism. First, we investigated
the copper−acetylide mechanism. As depicted in Figure 1, only
the most favorable pathway for the formation of the major
isomer is presented, while the energy profiles for the SR-
configured isomer (Figure S1) and R-configured pathway
(Figure S2) are provided in the Supporting Information.
Deprotonation of alkyne 1a in the active species Cu-I by
trifluoroacetylacetonate (Tfacac) yields copper−acetylide 5
associated with transition state 4-ts. The exothermic reaction
releases 2.2 kcal/mol energy with an energy barrier of 7.8 kcal/
mol. Subsequent carbenation proceeds via transition state 6-ts
through coordination of diazoacetate 2a, affording the
copper−carbene acetylide intermediate 7 accompanied by
releasing nitrogen gas. This intermediate undergoes carbene
insertion to form propargyl copper species 9 via transition state
8-ts. The energy barriers for nitrogen dissociation via transition
states 6-ts-R and 6-ts-S are 27.6 and 31.6 kcal/mol,
respectively. The relative Gibbs free energies of copper−
carbene acetylide species 7-R and 7-S are −1.8 and −2.3 kcal/
mol, respectively, indicating that carbenation is exothermic
under experimental conditions. The Cu−carbene bond length
in Fischer metal-carbene
63
species 7-S is 1.88 Å, suggesting a
covalent character. Furthermore, localized orbital bonding
analysis
61
shows that the oxidation state of Cu remains +1
through these processes. To confirm the reliability of the

The copper−carbene acetylide intermediate rapidly converts
into the more stable propargyl copper species, 9-R (ΔG =

respectively, indicating that the transformation of copper−
acetylide to copper−carbene acetylide is irreversible. There-
fore, these two steps determine the stereoselectivity of the
reaction. Re-face addition of 2a to the copper species yields the
R-isomer, whereas Si-face addition of 2a affords the S-isomer.

3.1.2. Copper−Carbene Mechanism. Next, we examined
the copper−carbene mechanism. Ligand exchange with the
diazo compound 2a yields complex 12, which is an endergonic
process at 28.9 kcal/mol (Scheme 4). Denitrogenation of
intermediate 12 proceeds associated with transition state 13-ts,
overcoming an energy barrier of 44.8 kcal/mol to form
copper−carbene intermediate 14. The coordinated terminal
alkyne 1a in intermediate 14 is deprotonated by Tfacac
through transition state 15-ts-S, resulting in the corresponding
copper−carbene acetylide 7-S with an energy barrier of 23.5
kcal/mol. Subsequent carbene insertion into the copper−
acetylide bond and protonation occur analogously to the
copper−acetylide mechanism.

reaction between copper−acetylide 5 and diazo 2a, leading to
the formation of R- and S-configured propargyl copper species.

the transition state and that stereoselectivity is primarily
determined by electrostatic interactions.
The above ASM analysis indicates that electrostatic
interactions play a key role in inducing stereoselectivity. To
further validate these interactions, a qualitative noncovalent
interaction (NCI) analysis
61
was performed on the transition
states 6-ts-R and 6-ts-S formed during nucleophilic addition.
The observed stereoselectivity in the carbenation process is
attributed to distinct noncovalent interaction patterns between
the prochiral faces, as illustrated by the optimized transition-
state geometries in Figure 2. We characterized these
interactions using two complementary methods: atom-in-
molecule (AIM) and NCI. In the AIM approach, bond critical
points (BCPs) and bond paths are identified to determine the
electrostatic interactions. The NCI method visualizes non-
covalent interactions through RDG isosurfaces. The electron
density (ρ) values at these BCPs provide a quantitative
measure for elucidating the strength of a specific interaction,
which are rendered by the AIM analysis. Together, the two
methods resolve ambiguities in interpreting atomic proximities
by differentiating the stabilizing interactions from geometric
artifacts. This dual analytical approach aligns with the ASM
analysis that supports the integration of AIM and NCI for
mapping interaction regions in stereoselective reactions.

3.3. Ligand Effects. The results in Section 3.2 demonstrate
that the chiral bisoxazoline (Box) ligand has an important
influence in determining the yield and stereoselectivity of the
cross-coupling reaction between diazo compounds and
terminal alkynes under copper catalysis. Additional calculations
involved in stereoselective transition states were carried out to
further elucidate the influences on the stereoselectivity of the
chiral ligand. The structures of ligands are shown in Figure S4
of the Supporting Information. The energy gap of the
stereoselective step is reduced to 3.5 kcal/mol by replacing
the Box ligand with a six-membered ring variant (Ligand-1,
Table 2), corresponding to a calculated ee of 99.5%. Switching
to a five-membered ring ligand (Ligand-2) further narrows this
energy gap to 1.5 kcal/mol, leading to diminished
enantioselectivity with only 85.4% ee. Moderate enantioselec-
tivity is observed when the Box ligand features a gem-dimethyl
linkage (Ligand-3) as well as the other two types of Box
ligands (Ligand-4 and Ligand-5). The computed ee values,
derived from the energy profiles, show reasonable agreement
with the experimental results. These computational insights

4. CONCLUSIONS
The DFT method was performed to explore the mechanism of
the cross-coupling reaction of diazoacetate and alkyne
catalyzed by Cu(I) species toward the synthesis of chiral
allenes. The proposed pathway comprises five key steps: (1)
alkynation of the Cu(I) species to form copper−acetylide
species, (2) carbenation of the diazoacetate to generate
copper−carbene acetylide species, (3) carbene insertion into
the copper−carbene acetylide species, yielding a propargyl
copper intermediate, (4) an intramolecular aldol reaction that
releases the allenoate copper species, and (5) protonation of
the allenoate copper species to afford the final chiral exocyclic
α-allenol and regenerate the active copper catalyst. The
carbenation step was identified as both the stereoselectivity-
and rate-determining step, with an energy barrier of 27.6 kcal/
mol. DFT calculations indicate that the copper−carbene
pathway exhibits an overall energy barrier of 44.8 kcal/mol
and is thus energetically disfavored. An NCI analysis revealed
the significance of interactions between diazoacetate and the
indane group of the Box ligand in governing the stereo-
selectivity. A range of chiral Box ligands was also evaluated,
and the presence of an indane group was found to promote
high stereoselectivity, consistent with experimental findings.
Computational results demonstrate that when an indane group
is present on the Box ligand, the conventional pathway
comprising alkynylation, carbenation, carbene insertion, aldol
reaction, and protonation is energetically favorable. The
present study enhances the mechanistic understanding of the
cross-coupling reaction between diazoacetate and alkyne
catalyzed by copper and offers a theoretical foundation for
guiding further experimental studies.

ABSTRACT: Terminal alkynes have emerged as highly versatile
building blocks for constructing C−C bonds. These compounds are
thought to undergo conversion to acetylide intermediates before
further transformation. In the present work, the possible reaction
mechanisms of the cross-coupling reaction of diazoacetate with
alkyne under copper catalysis are investigated using the M06-L
method. Two diferent reaction pathways including a copper−
acetylide mechanism and a copper−carbene mechanism are
investigated and comparatively analyzed. Computational results

demonstrate that the energetically favored pathway follows a copper-acetylide mechanism, comprising alkynation of the terminal
alkyne, carbenation, carbene insertion, Aldol reaction, and catalyst regeneration. In contrast, the alternative pathway involving a
carbenation−alkynation sequence is found to be less favorable. The rate-determining step is verified by the carbenation process,
which also determines the stereoselectivity. Noncovalent interaction (NCI) analysis reveals that noncovalent interactions between
the diazo and indane groups of the bisoxazoline ligand are important in controlling stereoselectivity. Calculations involving a series of
chiral ligands further demonstrate that the bulky indane moiety in the bisoxazoline ligand is essential for achieving stereoselectivity,
consistent with experimental observations.
1. INTRODUCTION

Terminal alkynes have garnered significant interest due to their
distinctive structural characteristics and high reactivity, making
them highly versatile building blocks for constructing C−C
bonds. These compounds are typically converted into acetylide
intermediates prior to further transformation.<sup>1−5</sup> Trans-
formation of terminal alkynes represents one of the most
efective strategies to construct multifunctional molecules from
simple precursors under transition-metal catalysis.<sup>6−14</sup> An
alkyne−metal complex forms through the coordination of a
transition metal to the alkyne triple bond. This interaction
weakens the triple bond and facilitates subsequent nucleophilic
attack, leading to the formation of a vinylmetal species
(Scheme 1). Additionally, this metal coordination enhances
the acidity of the terminal hydrogen, enabling deprotonation to
form an alkynyl−metal species.

Copper salts, valued for their low cost and minimal toxicity,
are extensively employed in organic transformations.<sup>15−22</sup>
Among their applications, copper-catalyzed cross-coupling
reactions involving terminal alkynes are well-established, and
numerous strategies have been devised for the construction of
allenes.<sup>23−30</sup> Recently, Sun et al. reported a tandem cross-
coupling/alkynylogous aldol reaction between terminal alkyne
and diazoacetate catalyzed by copper species for the synthesis
of tetrasubstituted allenes (Scheme 2).<sup>31</sup> This method afords
the products in a high yield (87%, Scheme 2) with excellent

Transition Metal (TM) Catalysis

enantioselectivity (97% ee, Scheme 2) and diastereoselectivity
(>19:1 dr, Scheme 2), representing an eficient approach for
the enantioselective synthesis of tetrasubstituted allenes
bearing both central and axial chirality.

The catalytic copper species typically activates the terminal
alkyne to produce a copper−acetylide species and also
activates the diazoacetate to produce a copper−carbene

Diazoacetate with a Terminal Alkyne

species. Terminal alkyne undergoes deprotonation to deliver
the copper−acetylide, which subsequently reacts with the
diazoacetate. Alternatively, the copper catalyst may first
activate the diazoacetate to produce the copper−carbene,
which then engages with the terminal alkyne. Although Sun
and co-workers have made significant progress to elucidate the
mechanism of this reaction, two major problems are still
unclear. First, establishing a general mechanistic scheme is
challenging due to the involvement of diferent activation
modes. Second, the molecular origin of the high stereo-
selectivity requires further clarification. As a result, our interest
was drawn to investigating this copper-catalyzed asymmetric
synthesis of a tetrasubstituted allene. Theoretical mechanistic
analysis of transition-metal-catalyzed reactions<sup>32−37</sup>
is at the
center of our research. Therefore, in this study, we employed
density functional theory (DFT), which is a robust computa-
tional method for mechanistic investigations,<sup>38−49</sup>
to theoret-
ically investigate the mechanism of the copper-catalyzed cross-
coupling reaction between a terminal alkyne and diazoacetate.
In particular, we intend to elucidate the activation mode in
detail, specifically whether copper−acetylide or copper−
carbene serves as the key intermediate.
2. COMPUTATIONAL METHODS

All quantum chemical calculations were performed using the Gaussian
09 software package.<sup>50</sup> Geometry optimizations were carried out with
the M06-L functional.<sup>51,52</sup> The 6-31G(d, p) basis set<sup>53,54</sup>
was
employed for the C, H, O, N, and F atoms, while the SDD basis
set<sup>55,56</sup> was used for the Cu atom. Solvation efects were incorporated
via the continuum solvation model IEF-PCM,<sup>57,58</sup>
using dichloro-
methane (DCM, ε = 8.93) as the solvent. Harmonic vibrational
analysis verifies that the stationary points are characterized as minima
with no imaginary frequency or transition states with one and only
one imaginary frequency, respectively. To refine the calculated energy,
single-point calculations with a larger basis set were then performed
based on these optimized structures, by using the M06-L functional
with the Def2-TZVP basis set.<sup>59,60</sup> The free energies reported in this
work were calculated based on the single point energy at the M06-L/
def2-TZVP level, including the Gibbs free energy thermal correction
obtained from vibrational analysis at the geometry optimization level.
For disclosing the origin of stereoselectivity, the Multiwfn software
package<sup>61</sup> is used to generate the interaction wave functions, which
are then visualized through VMD

3.1. Reaction Mechanism. Considering the behavior of
copper species, we propose both the copper−acetylide
mechanism and the copper−carbene mechanism on the
copper-catalyzed reaction between diazoacetate and alkyne,
as illustrated in Scheme 3. Both pathways were initiated from
the Cu-I species. In the copper−acetylide mechanism, the

Subsequent carbenation between Int-I and diazoacetate 2a

α-allenol and regenerates the active copper species. With these
proposed mechanisms in hand, theoretical calculations were
conducted to elucidate the detailed mechanism of the Cu(I)-
catalyzed cross-coupling reaction between diazoacetate and
alkyne.

3.1.1. Copper−Acetylide Mechanism. First, we investigated
the copper−acetylide mechanism. As depicted in Figure 1, only

Deprotonation of alkyne 1a in the active species Cu-I by

8-ts. The energy barriers for nitrogen dissociation via transition

carbene acetylide species 7-R and 7-S are −1.8 and −2.3 kcal/

covalent character. Furthermore, localized orbital bonding

through these processes. To confirm the reliability of the

4. CONCLUSIONS

The DFT method was performed to explore the mechanism of
the cross-coupling reaction of diazoacetate and alkyne
catalyzed by Cu(I) species toward the synthesis of chiral
allenes. The proposed pathway comprises five key steps: (1)
alkynation of the Cu(I) species to form copper−acetylide
species, (2) carbenation of the diazoacetate to generate
copper−carbene acetylide species, (3) carbene insertion into
the copper−carbene acetylide species, yielding a propargyl
copper intermediate, (4) an intramolecular aldol reaction that
releases the allenoate copper species, and (5) protonation of
the allenoate copper species to aford the final chiral exocyclic
α-allenol and regenerate the active copper catalyst. The
carbenation step was identified as both the stereoselectivity-
and rate-determining step, with an energy barrier of 27.6 kcal/
mol. DFT calculations indicate that the copper−carbene

pathway exhibits an overall energy barrier of 44.8 kcal/mol
and is thus energetically disfavored. An NCI analysis revealed
the significance of interactions between diazoacetate and the
indane group of the Box ligand in governing the stereo-
selectivity. A range of chiral Box ligands was also evaluated,
and the presence of an indane group was found to promote
high stereoselectivity, consistent with experimental findings.
Computational results demonstrate that when an indane group
is present on the Box ligand, the conventional pathway
comprising alkynylation, carbenation, carbene insertion, aldol
reaction, and protonation is energetically favorable. The
present study enhances the mechanistic understanding of the
cross-coupling reaction between diazoacetate and alkyne
catalyzed by copper and ofers a theoretical foundation for
guiding further experimental studies.
